definition: A way of describing where energy is held in a system — e.g. kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic.
clues: This is a way of categorising energy in a system
There are eight types in GCSE physics
Kinetic and thermal are examples
A named type of energy held by an object or system — e.g. kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, thermal, nuclear

definition: Energy stored in a moving object. KE = ½mv². Depends on both the mass and the speed of the object.
clues: This is a type of energy store
It is associated with moving objects
Its equation involves mass and speed squared
Energy stored in a moving object — KE = ½mv²; doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy

definition: Energy stored in an object due to its height above the ground. GPE = mgh. Increases as an object is lifted higher.
clues: This is a type of energy store
It is associated with an object's height
Its equation involves mass, g and height
Energy stored in an object due to its position above the ground — GPE = mgh; the higher it is, the more energy stored

definition: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object, such as a spring. Elastic PE = ½ke².
clues: This is a type of energy store
It is found in stretched or compressed objects
Springs, rubber bands and elastic are examples
Energy stored in a deformed elastic object — ½ke²; released when the object returns to its original shape

definition: Energy stored in the movement of particles within an object. Objects with more internal energy are at a higher temperature.
clues: This is a type of energy store
It is related to the temperature of an object
Hotter objects have more of this
Energy held in the random motion of particles within an object — the greater it is, the higher the temperature

definition: Energy stored in the bonds of chemical compounds, such as fuels and food. Released during chemical reactions.
clues: This is a type of energy store
It is found in fuels and food
It is released during chemical reactions
Energy stored in chemical bonds — released during combustion, respiration and other exothermic reactions

definition: The movement of energy from one store to another, by one of four pathways: mechanically, electrically, by heating, or by radiation.
clues: This describes how energy moves between stores
There are four main pathways
Mechanical work, heating and radiation are examples
Energy moves from one store to another via a pathway — mechanical work, electrical work, heating or radiation (light/sound)

definition: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred from one store to another. The total energy in a closed system is always constant.
clues: This is a fundamental law of physics
Energy can never be created or destroyed
It can only change from one form to another
The total energy in a closed system stays the same — energy is only ever transferred, not made or lost

definition: The fraction of the total energy input that is usefully transferred. Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. Can be expressed as a decimal or percentage.
clues: This is a measure of how well a device uses energy
It compares useful output to total input
It is always less than 1 (or 100%)
Useful energy output ÷ total energy input — no device is 100% efficient as some energy is always wasted as heat or sound

definition: Energy transferred to an unwanted store — usually thermal (heat) or sound. It dissipates into the surroundings and is difficult to recover.
clues: This is energy transferred to an unhelpful store
It usually ends up as heat or sound
It reduces the efficiency of a device
Energy that ends up in an unwanted store — usually heat or sound — reducing the useful output of a device

definition: A diagram used to represent energy transfers in a device. The width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy it represents.
clues: This is a type of diagram used in physics
It shows how energy is transferred in a device
The width of the arrows represents the amount of energy
An energy flow diagram where arrow widths are proportional to the energy amount — shows useful and wasted energy at a glance

definition: The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done. P = E/t or P = W/t. Measured in watts (W).
clues: This is a measure of how quickly energy is transferred
Its unit is the watt
It equals energy divided by time
The rate of energy transfer — P = E/t; a 100 W bulb transfers 100 joules of energy every second

definition: The SI unit of power. 1 watt = 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s).
clues: This is a unit of measurement in physics
It is the unit of power
1 of these equals 1 joule per second
The SI unit of power — 1 W = 1 J/s; named after James Watt

definition: The SI unit of energy and work. Symbol: J. 1 joule = 1 newton × 1 metre.
clues: This is a unit of measurement in physics
It is the unit of energy and work
1 of these equals 1 newton-metre
The SI unit of energy — 1 J = 1 N·m; named after James Prescott Joule

definition: An energy resource that is naturally replenished and will not run out, such as solar, wind, tidal, wave, geothermal and hydroelectric power.
clues: This is a type of energy resource
It will not run out
Solar, wind and tidal are examples
An energy source that is continuously replaced by natural processes — solar, wind, wave, tidal, hydroelectric and geothermal

definition: An energy resource that is being used faster than it is being replaced and will eventually run out. Examples: fossil fuels and nuclear fuel.
clues: This is a type of energy resource
It will eventually run out
Fossil fuels are examples
An energy source used faster than it is naturally replaced — coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuel are all examples

definition: A non-renewable fuel formed from the remains of ancient organisms over millions of years. Examples: coal, oil and natural gas.
clues: This is a type of non-renewable fuel
It was formed from ancient organisms over millions of years
Coal, oil and natural gas are examples
Fuels formed from ancient marine or plant remains over millions of years — coal, oil and natural gas; all release CO₂ when burned

definition: A non-renewable energy resource (typically uranium or plutonium) that releases energy through nuclear fission. Produces no CO₂ but creates radioactive waste.
clues: This is a type of non-renewable fuel
It uses nuclear fission to release energy
Uranium is a common example
A fuel that releases energy by nuclear fission rather than combustion — no CO₂ produced but radioactive waste is a challenge

definition: The network of cables, pylons and transformers that distributes electrical energy from power stations to homes and businesses across the country.
clues: This is a system for distributing electricity
It uses pylons, cables and transformers
It connects power stations to homes and businesses
The network distributing electricity nationwide — uses step-up transformers at power stations and step-down transformers near consumers to minimise energy loss

definition: A device that converts light energy from the Sun into electrical energy (photovoltaic cells) or thermal energy (solar thermal panels).
clues: This is a renewable energy device
It converts energy from the Sun
It can produce electricity or heat water
A device that captures solar energy — photovoltaic cells produce electricity; solar thermal panels heat water directly

definition: A device that converts the kinetic energy of wind into electrical energy using a generator.
clues: This is a renewable energy device
It uses moving air to generate electricity
It has large rotating blades
A structure with rotating blades driven by wind — the kinetic energy of wind is converted into electrical energy via a generator

definition: Electricity generated by using the gravitational potential energy of water stored in a high reservoir to drive turbines as it flows down.
clues: This is a renewable energy resource
It uses water stored at height
The water drives turbines as it flows down
GPE of water in a high reservoir is converted to kinetic energy as it falls through turbines — generating electricity with no fuel costs

definition: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Symbol: c. Equation: Q = mcΔT. Unit: J/kg°C.
clues: This is a property of materials
It measures how much energy is needed to heat a substance
Its unit is J/kg°C
The energy required to heat 1 kg of a material by 1°C — used in Q = mcΔT to calculate thermal energy changes

definition: Materials or methods used to reduce the rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction, convection or radiation, keeping buildings or objects warm.
clues: This describes materials or methods that reduce heat loss
It slows conduction, convection and radiation
Loft insulation and cavity wall insulation are examples
Reducing the rate of heat transfer from a building or object — e.g. loft insulation, double glazing, cavity wall insulation

definition: The time it takes for an energy resource or efficiency measure to save as much energy as was used to produce or install it.
clues: This is a concept in energy economics
It is the time taken for an investment to break even in energy terms
It is used to compare the value of different energy-saving measures
The time for an installation to save as much energy as it cost to produce — used to evaluate the economic and environmental value of insulation and renewables
